evaluation.positioning_hook: A group of orphaned teens escape a sinister facility, take refuge with a guarded stranger, and accidentally unlock powers that put them back in the crosshairs of the woman who created them.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The orphaned-kids-on-the-run engine is easy to grasp and the powers reveal gives the premise a commercial lift. The current draft is still more raw than broadly market-ready, with the appeal concentrated in genre buyers rather than a wide four-quadrant audience.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The core setup is visible: children escape an abusive orphanage/lab and end up in a new danger cycle. But the script reads like an outline across multiple versions of the story, so the hook lands late and then keeps shifting.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Harper and Marissa have a clear escape impulse, Ethan has volatility and illness, and Nina has a protective outsider energy. They function, but the draft is still defining who the true center is and what each character uniquely brings beyond the situation.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The orphanage-as-experiment-farm angle has some bite, and the body-horror testing imagery is memorable. The broader execution still leans familiar, with the draft moving through recognizable escape, shelter, and powers beats without a fully ownable voice yet.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The opening lab sequence has urgency, but the script then resets into repeated escape-and-hide beats and a later section that reads like notes rather than finished scenes. The momentum is interrupted by structural placeholders, which makes escalation hard to track.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The combination of children, medical experimentation, and a hidden powers reveal has a built-in genre promise. What keeps it from landing higher is that the emotional and mythic logic is still broad rather than inevitable.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The orphanage/lab has a clear oppressive function, but the surrounding world is still thinly sketched. Nina’s house adds a second setting with some texture, yet the larger social system around the kids remains mostly implied.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script toggles between earnest kid-drama, body-horror, and superhero-origin material, but the tonal blend is not yet controlled. Scenes like the dinner conversation and the bone-dislocation sequence sit in very different registers without a stable signature.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are seeds of deeper material in Mother Logan’s guilt, Ethan’s illness, and Marissa’s hidden age/identity. The draft hints at more beneath the surface, but it has not yet organized those threads into a strong slow-burn architecture.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The kids have a workable group dynamic, especially Harper/Marissa and the friction around Ethan, and Nina gives the ensemble a new relational center. The relationships are active enough to generate scenes, though the cast is still too broad and underdefined for the ensemble to feel fully engine-driven.

lead_characters.name: Harper
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid-to-late teens, orphaned, likely Black or unspecified ethnicity as written.
lead_characters.hook: The youngest of the escapees, Harper is the emotional engine of the group: observant, brave when it counts, and more willing than the others to trust people and push forward. She wants out, but she also wants everyone else to survive the exit, which makes her the script’s clearest moral center.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Millie Bobby Brown in Stranger Things — a young lead who can carry fear, resolve, and leadership in the same scene. The role gives an actor the chance to play innocence under pressure while becoming the person the group follows.

lead_characters.name: Marissa
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late teens, orphaned, age-revealed as 18 though she believes she is still a minor.
lead_characters.hook: Marissa reads as the older sister in the group even before the script reveals her hidden age, which gives her a built-in contradiction: cautious, conflict-avoidant, but finally ready to move. Her relationship to Harper is protective and practical, and her secret age gives her a useful identity wrinkle.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Kaitlyn Dever in Short Term 12 a chance to play guarded intelligence with emotional restraint. It offers an actor a quiet authority part that can turn into a major reveal when the age/identity truth lands.

lead_characters.name: Ethan
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late teens, sickly, physically compromised, orphaned/escaped subject.
lead_characters.hook: Ethan is the volatile wildcard: sick, irritable, self-isolating, and clearly carrying more history than he wants to share. His illness and pain make him unpredictable, but the script also positions him as the one with the most immediate survival instinct and the most dangerous edge.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Lucas Hedges in Manchester by the Sea — a young man whose internal damage shows up in behavior, not speeches. The role gives an actor a chance to play fragility, menace, and reluctant protectiveness in the same frame.

lead_characters.name: Mother Logan
lead_characters.demographics: Female, middle-aged, authority figure, caretaker/administrator of the orphanage-lab.
lead_characters.hook: Mother Logan is the story’s human face of institutional cruelty: controlling, manipulative, and increasingly trapped by the consequences of her own choices. The script gives her a guilt thread and a physical collapse, which makes her more than a stock villain even as she remains the primary threat.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that let Toni Collette in Hereditary move from authority to terror to grief without leaving the frame. It gives an actor a full-spectrum turn: maternal presence, moral rot, and body-horror breakdown.

lead_characters.name: Nina
lead_characters.demographics: Female, adult, homeowner, childless, emotionally guarded but nurturing.
lead_characters.hook: Nina is the refuge character who immediately complicates the escape story: warm enough to invite the kids in, but armed, watchful, and carrying her own grief around motherhood. She has the strongest adult-humanity on the page outside Mother Logan, and her house becomes the first real alternative to the orphanage.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Regina King in If Beale Street Could Talk or Aunjanue Ellis in King Richard — a grounded adult role that can hold tenderness, authority, and pain at once. It gives an actor a chance to be the emotional shelter of the film without becoming passive.

lead_characters.name: Unknown Man
lead_characters.demographics: Male, adult, unseen/partially obscured, criminal or institutional power broker.
lead_characters.hook: The Unknown Man is a pressure source more than a person on the page right now, but he matters because he keeps Mother Logan in line and appears to have hired the men in suits. His anonymity gives the story a conspiracy layer, even if the draft has not yet fully defined his function.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of voice-and-presence role that can become a memorable menace if cast with the right actor, similar to Javier Bardem in No Country for Old Men in terms of controlled threat. The appeal is the chance to create authority without overexposure.

lead_characters.name: Candace
lead_characters.hook: Candace is one of the younger kids who helps make the escape group feel like a real found family rather than a two- or three-person unit. She is scared, reactive, and useful as a barometer for the danger around them.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a young-performer role with clear emotional business, similar to the child ensemble energy in Room or The Florida Project. It gives an actor a chance to play fear and dependency without needing a huge speech load.

lead_characters.name: Blake
lead_characters.hook: Blake is the blunt one, the kid most willing to say what the others are thinking, which gives the group some texture. He reads as skeptical and undernourished by the orphanage life, and his cynicism helps sell the emotional damage of the place.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a good young-actor role in the vein of the sharper kids in Stand by Me or The Florida Project. It offers a performer a chance to land attitude and vulnerability in the same beat.

lead_characters.name: Justin
lead_characters.hook: Justin is quieter and more observant, with a soft-spoken loyalty to Tom that gives him a defined relational anchor. He helps round out the younger ensemble and gives the house scenes a calmer, more watchful energy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting child role that benefits from subtlety rather than big swings, similar to the quieter ensemble work in Beasts of the Southern Wild. It gives a young actor a chance to play internalized loyalty.

lead_characters.name: Tom
lead_characters.hook: Tom is Justin’s counterpart and seems to function as the more hesitant half of that pair. The script uses him to reinforce the group’s dependence on one another and to keep the younger ensemble from feeling interchangeable.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a useful young-ensemble role for an actor who can play hesitation and attachment without overexplaining it. It has the kind of naturalistic texture that can stand out in a child cast.

lead_characters.name: George
lead_characters.hook: George is the detail-oriented kid who likes to draw, which gives him the beginnings of a personality beyond survival. He is also the one most likely to blurt out the truth, making him a useful pressure valve in group scenes.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets a young actor play specificity instead of generic fear, similar to the more idiosyncratic kids in Eighth Grade or The Florida Project. The drawing detail gives the performance a memorable hook.

lead_characters.name: Will
lead_characters.hook: Will is the hopeful one, the kid who still responds to reassurance and talks about gifts and being taken care of. He gives the group a little innocence, which makes the orphanage damage feel more acute.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a child-role showcase for tenderness, similar to the more vulnerable kids in Room. It gives a young actor a chance to play need and optimism without becoming saccharine.

lead_characters.name: Trisha
lead_characters.demographics: Female, adult, orphanage staff or adjacent caretaker.
lead_characters.hook: Trisha appears briefly as someone who may be wavering on the system, which makes her a useful moral contrast to Mother Logan. Her presence suggests there are adults inside the machine who are not fully committed to it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a compact but playable supporting role for an actor who can suggest a larger off-screen life quickly, similar to the kind of brief but loaded turns in prison or institution dramas. It gives a performer a chance to imply conscience under pressure.

lead_characters.name: John
lead_characters.demographics: Male, adult, orphanage staff or adjacent caretaker.
lead_characters.hook: John is paired with Trisha and reads as another adult caught between complicity and fear. His brief attempt to pull away from the situation gives the scene a human crack in the institution.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a small but functional role for an actor who can make a single scene feel lived-in, like the supporting turns in elevated genre pieces. The appeal is in playing panic and regret fast.

casting_characteristics: ensemble of child performers with distinct age bands

technical.vfx_details: The current pages are mostly practical, with the main effects burden coming from body-horror makeup and the later powers reveal in the abandoned lab.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical blood effects, bone-dislocation makeup/prosthetics, syringe-machine effects, and a physical fight beat in Nina's house.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model; best suited to a contained genre launch with franchise optionality only if the powers mythology is expanded later.

budget.note: Contemporary locations, a small cast, and mostly practical effects keep the spend contained; the main cost pressure is the body-horror makeup and the abandoned-lab sequence.

casting.note: The project depends on a strong teen ensemble, a credible child cast, and an adult actress who can play Mother Logan as both caretaker and threat. Ethan and Harper in particular need performers who can carry fear, anger, and vulnerability without flattening.

development.note: The draft reads like a hybrid of screenplay and outline, with Act III still in note form and the central mythology only partially defined. A buyer will immediately flag the need for a cleaner protagonist spine, a finished third act, and a more settled genre identity.

comp_set.title: The New Mutants
comp_set.why_it_comps: Teen characters trapped in a facility, body-horror experimentation, and powers emerging out of trauma put this in the same youth-genre lane.

comp_set.title: The Darkest Minds
comp_set.why_it_comps: Orphaned or displaced young people with abilities on the run from an institution maps closely to the script's escape-and-survival engine.

comp_set.title: Room
comp_set.why_it_comps: The emotional DNA of children escaping captivity and learning the outside world gives this a similar survival-and-recovery core.

comp_set.title: Chronicle
comp_set.why_it_comps: The powers-origin beat and found-footing of discovery through experimentation echo the same low-to-mid-budget genre appeal.

audience_target.primary_audience: Genre viewers who like teen survival stories with a darker sci-fi edge and an emotional found-family core.
audience_target.demographics: Teens through adults 18-34, with secondary appeal to 35+ genre audiences who respond to elevated YA and contained sci-fi thrillers.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary settings, a modest ensemble, and practical effects keep this in indie-feature territory, with the abandoned lab and body-horror sequence as the main scope drivers.

lane_fit.detail: The script sits naturally in the lane of contained, character-forward genre features that can sell on premise, young cast energy, and a clear visual hook. The orphanage/lab setup and powers reveal give it enough genre identity to attract buyers looking for a darker YA-adjacent swing.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature as written; the current draft does not yet define a spinoff vector beyond a general powers mythology.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Orphanage-as-lab is a clean genre engine.
strengths.what_it_means: That premise gives the project an immediate commercial identity: kids in danger, institutional abuse, and a built-in mystery box around what the orphanage is really doing. Buyers who want a contained elevated-genre feature can understand the movie in one sentence.
strengths.evidence: The opening laboratory sequence, the serum testing on Ethan and Mother Logan, and the guards moving the children back into the system all establish the engine fast.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Mother Logan has real villain gravity.
strengths.what_it_means: The role is not just a generic authority figure; she carries guilt, control, and physical collapse, which makes the antagonist lane more castable and more memorable. That is the kind of part that can attract an actor looking for a prestige-leaning genre turn.
strengths.evidence: She orders the testing, insists on staying to watch, then volunteers herself as the test subject and later breaks down as the side effects hit.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The kid ensemble gives the film a found-family spine.
strengths.what_it_means: The group dynamic creates audience attachment beyond the central mystery, which is valuable for both word-of-mouth and casting. A buyer can see a young ensemble that can carry fear, loyalty, and escape momentum.
strengths.evidence: Harper pushes the others to leave, Marissa takes on the protective older-sister role, and the younger kids each get a small personality marker in the house scenes.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The body-horror testing sequence is memorable.
strengths.what_it_means: The physical mutation beat gives the script a visual signature that can separate it from softer YA escape stories. That kind of practical-effects moment is useful for trailers, festival programming, and genre marketing.
strengths.evidence: Mother Logan’s arm bumps, muscle spasms, and bone dislocations create a concrete, unsettling payoff to the serum test.

whats_special.headline: This has the bones of a contained, youth-driven sci-fi thriller: a sinister orphanage, a memorable body-horror turn, and a teen ensemble that can sell found-family emotion. If the third act is fully realized, the package could fit the exact lane buyers use for elevated genre features with practical effects and breakout-young-cast upside.

items.area: The draft still reads like an outline.
items.detail: Act III is presented as notes and alternate ideas rather than finished scenes, which is the biggest greenlight obstacle on the page. Buyers will see the premise and the imagery, but they will also see that the actual feature spine is not yet locked.

Harper is framed as the bravest, Marissa gets the oldest-sister energy, Ethan drives the most volatile scenes, and Mother Logan briefly dominates the opening. That diffusion makes it harder to know whose movie this is, which matters in a feature sale.

items.area: The genre identity is still in transition.
items.detail: The pages move from institutional thriller to body horror to powers-origin sci-fi, and the tonal handoff is not yet controlled. That is workable in development, but on the page it reads as three adjacent movies rather than one settled lane.

items.area: The child ensemble is broad for the page count.
items.detail: Harper, Marissa, Ethan, Candace, Blake, Justin, Tom, Will, and George all need to register, but several are still defined by one trait or one line. That creates casting and development friction because the emotional weight is spread across more roles than the draft fully supports.

issues.headline: The core premise is commercial, but the script is still carrying outline-level structure and a shifting lead focus, which will be the first two conversations in any buyer room. The ensemble and genre blend are promising, but they need a finished feature spine before the package can really travel.
